records.cutoff: 2011, after a bacterial RNA-guided nuclease system and two required RNA components are known, before the 2012 programmable single-guide cleavage result

bet.dominantBottleneck: The minimal programmable mechanism is unresolved because no purified system has yet demonstrated that the large nuclease plus the two small RNAs are sufficient to cleave a chosen DNA target in a sequence-directed manner.

routes.route: Purified-component in-vitro RNA-guided cleavage
routes.reason: Directly tests sufficiency of the known components and makes the programmable recognition mechanism accessible to biochemical dissection.

routes.route: Design and test a single-guide RNA chimera
routes.reason: If the two-RNA reaction is reconstituted, fusing the trans-acting RNA to the target guide simplifies transfer and can be validated in the same cleavage assay.

routes.route: Heterologous plasmid-interference assay in E. coli
routes.reason: Defer until in-vitro cleavage is shown, because host interference cannot distinguish direct nuclease activity from accessory bacterial factors.

routes.route: Mismatch-panel specificity mapping
routes.reason: Quantifying cleavage against a panel of single- and multi-base mismatches is essential before claiming sequence-specific programmable cleavage.

routes.route: ZFN/TALEN-based cellular editing comparison
routes.reason: Transfection of cultured cells should wait until a molecular RNA-guided cleavage operation is reproducibly established outside cells.

bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Incubate recombinant large nuclease with in-vitro transcribed or chemically synthesized crRNA and tracrRNA and a linearized plasmid containing the complementary protospacer, then analyze for site-specific cleavage products by gel electrophoresis; include no-RNA, non-target guide, and tracrRNA-only negative controls.
requiredComplements: recombinant expression and purification of the large nuclease
in-vitro transcribed or synthetic crRNA and tracrRNA
cloned linearized target DNA with a known protospacer-adjacent motif if the system requires one
denaturing or agarose gel readout for cleavage fragments
mismatched target controls to evaluate specificity
mainFailureRisks: nucleolytic activity may require an unanticipated bacterial cofactor absent from the purified system
the two RNA components may require post-transcriptional processing or a specific processing nuclease
the large nuclease may be insoluble or require special buffer and ion conditions
cleavage may be observed only at high concentrations or with slow kinetics, making transfer impractical
in-vitro DNA cleavage may not predict safe or efficient editing in eukaryotic cells
bet.generalizationBoundary: Reconstituted RNA-guided cleavage in vitro supports a programmable nuclease mechanism, but does not by itself claim genome-editing safety, cellular delivery, or repair outcomes in eukaryotic cells.
unresolvedUnknowns: minimum sequence and structural requirements of each RNA and nuclease
whether a protospacer-adjacent motif or other flanking-sequence constraint determines target selection
whether the system cuts both DNA strands and if cleavage is staggered or blunt
which divalent metal ions and buffer conditions support maximal activity
how off-target tolerance scales with guide length and mismatches
whether heterologous expression in non-native hosts preserves activity
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: Proposed tests use only microbial genetics and sequencing, component purification, RNA synthesis and modification, in-vitro cleavage assays, and the stated contemporary editing baseline; no unavailable future tools are assumed.

records.cutoff: 2011, after a bacterial RNA-guided nuclease system and two required RNA components are known, before the 2012 programmable single-guide cleavage result

bet.dominantBottleneck: Biochemical specificity is unproven, blocking any transferable programmable-nuclease claim.

routes.route: Reconstitute programmable slicing in vitro
routes.reason: This directly tests whether the nuclease and two RNAs are sufficient for complementarity-dependent cleavage, which is the core unresolved claim.

routes.route: Minimal genetic system transfer in a heterologous bacterium
routes.reason: This introduces host-factor assumptions and is less diagnostic than biochemistry until the purified minimal reaction is established.

routes.route: Chimeric guide engineering for altered targets
routes.reason: Guide modularity should be tested only after the native reaction is reconstituted; early failures could be due to misfolding or missing cofactors rather than design principles.

routes.route: Structure-function mutagenesis of nuclease/RNA domains
routes.reason: This is mechanistically informative but requires a defined cleavage assay first to score mutants reliably.

routes.route: Compare to ZF/TALEN editing after nuclease operation
routes.reason: Transfection and genome editing are premature until molecular cleavage specificity is established and the system is transferred into a cellular context safely.

bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Run in vitro cleavage assays with purified nuclease, cognate trans-acting RNA, and synthetic target-derived guide RNA; test complementarity-dependent cleavage and scrambled/mismatched target controls.
requiredComplements: Purify recombinant nuclease
Synthesize guide and trans-acting RNAs
Use radiolabeled or fluorescent DNA/RNA substrates
Verify guide-trans-RNA-nuclease complex assembly by native gel
Include divalent metal and buffer conditions suitable for nuclease activity

The trans-acting RNA may adopt a different conformation in vitro
The native target is RNA rather than DNA, so the chosen substrate is wrong
Cleavage occurs but is poorly sequence-specific, undermining programmability
bet.generalizationBoundary: Any demonstrated cleavage applies only to this reconstituted locus with synthetic components in vitro; it does not establish genome-editing safety, cellular repair outcomes, or generalizability to other loci.
unresolvedUnknowns: Whether the trans-acting RNA is a scaffold, an allosteric activator, or a guide-processing factor
Whether there is a protospacer-adjacent motif or secondary structure requirement
Whether the natural target is DNA, RNA, or both
How off-target cleavage and cellular repair would behave in mammalian cells
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed actions stay within the listed capabilities: microbial genetics, protein/RNA purification, RNA synthesis, in vitro cleavage assays, and ZF/TALEN baseline comparisons; cell transfection is deferred until molecular specificity is established.

records.cutoff: 2011, after a bacterial RNA-guided nuclease system and two required RNA components are known, before the 2012 programmable single-guide cleavage result

bet.dominantBottleneck: The minimal programmable mechanism is unresolved: it is unknown whether the large nuclease plus the two RNA components are sufficient to specify sequence-targeted cleavage, or whether additional bacterial factors and RNA processing steps are required.

routes.route: In vitro minimal reconstitution
routes.reason: Purify the large nuclease, synthesize crRNA and tracrRNA, and test sequence-specific cleavage of a DNA substrate in a defined biochemical system to establish the core mechanism.

routes.route: Native-locus genetic dissection
routes.reason: Use microbial genetics in the natural host to confirm which components are necessary and to identify accessible mutants that perturb RNA processing or nuclease activity.

routes.route: Accessory-factor co-purification
routes.reason: If minimal reconstitution fails, identify additional bacterial factors by pulling down the nuclease-RNA complex or using genetic suppressors to restore activity.

routes.route: RNA maturation and minimal guide mapping
routes.reason: Test whether the two RNAs require processing by host RNases, and define the minimal functional regions of each RNA for guide loading and target recognition.

routes.route: Cell-culture transfer attempt
routes.reason: Defer transfection into cultured cells until a biochemical operation is demonstrated; otherwise off-target and repair artifacts cannot be interpreted.

bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: In vitro cleavage assay: incubate purified large nuclease with in vitro-transcribed crRNA containing a designed target-complementary sequence, tracrRNA, and a linear or supercoiled DNA substrate containing the matching protospacer plus a candidate PAM; assay for site-specific cleavage by gel electrophoresis against non-complementary and no-RNA controls. If cleavage is absent, supplement with native host lysate or candidate accessory factors to discriminate between intrinsic nuclease activity and host-factor dependence.
requiredComplements: Define the PAM or target-adjacent sequence requirement by screening small randomized libraries
Map minimal functional domains of crRNA and tracrRNA through truncation and mutation series
Validate programmability by swapping guide sequences to cleave multiple distinct targets
Confirm cleavage products by denaturing gel and Sanger sequencing
Use a catalytically inactivated nuclease mutant as a binding-only control
Test whether a single fused guide RNA can replace the two-RNA system
mainFailureRisks: The nuclease may be inactive when expressed heterologously without a bacterial chaperone or post-translational modification
The two RNAs may require in vivo processing by host RNases, making in vitro transcribed RNAs non-functional
Target recognition may depend on an unknown PAM-like motif, causing false-negative cleavage results
The nuclease may cleave non-specifically or have high off-target activity, complicating later cellular use
Cleavage alone may not lead to editing if cellular DNA repair pathways do not yield the desired outcome
Accessory proteins may be strictly required, preventing transfer to foreign hosts
bet.generalizationBoundary: A successful in vitro reconstitution would establish programmable RNA-guided DNA cleavage by the purified nuclease and two RNAs in a defined biochemical setting, but it would not establish safe or efficient genome editing in eukaryotic cells, low off-target activity, or delivery efficacy in living systems.
unresolvedUnknowns: Whether bacterial accessory factors are required for guide loading or target cleavage
The exact PAM or target-adjacent sequence required for cleavage
Whether the two-RNA system can be simplified to a single guide RNA
How the system behaves on chromatinized or eukaryotic DNA templates
What DNA repair pathways dominate after cleavage in different cell types
Off-target tolerance and specificity determinants beyond seed complementarity
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed actions stay within available capabilities: microbial genetics and sequencing, protein purification/reconstitution, RNA synthesis and modification, in-vitro cleavage assays, and ZF/TALEN as a baseline. Cultured-cell transfection is deferred until a molecular operation is biochemically established, respecting the stated constraints.

records.cutoff: late 2003, after large commodity clusters and a fault-tolerant distributed filesystem are described, before the MapReduce publication

bet.dominantBottleneck: Repeated reinvention of distributed execution logic: partitioning, scheduling, data movement, retries, and straggler handling are rebuilt by each application team.

routes.route: Build a map/reduce runtime with automatic partitioning, scheduling, retries, and locality-aware placement.
routes.reason: Directly targets the bottleneck by giving programmers only custom map and reduce functions while the runtime handles distribution, failure, and locality.

routes.route: Extend the distributed filesystem with server-side aggregation/merge operations.
routes.reason: Could reduce data movement for simple aggregate cases but couples storage semantics to job logic and makes custom record transformations harder to express.

routes.route: Adopt a relational SQL-style cluster query engine with user-defined functions.
routes.reason: Relational abstraction may be too rigid for append-heavy scans, custom map-style transformations, and non-relational data formats; benchmark a representative job before committing.

routes.route: Provide a reusable library for manual pipeline management.
routes.reason: A library still leaves programmers responsible for machine assignment, retries, data movement, and stragglers; it relieves symptoms rather than eliminating the reinvention burden.

routes.route: Design a general multi-stage dataflow DAG with explicit operators.
routes.reason: More expressive for complex pipelines but significantly harder to build and debug; first validate whether a simple map/reduce model captures enough production workloads.

bet.topRoute: Build a map/reduce runtime with automatic partitioning, scheduling, retries, and locality-aware placement.
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Run a controlled comparison on a large production-like scan-and-aggregate job using three implementations: the map/reduce runtime, a minimal SQL-over-cluster prototype, and the existing manual pipeline; inject random worker failures, measure end-to-end time, local vs remote bytes read, restart overhead, and programmer lines of code, then check whether map/reduce meets locality and failure tolerance without custom scheduling logic.
requiredComplements: fault-tolerant distributed filesystem with block locality information
job scheduler and worker process management
partition and group/aggregate runtime components
failure detection and task retry mechanisms
straggler detection and backup task execution
representative production batch workloads and metrics collection
mainFailureRisks: map/reduce is too restrictive for iterative or multi-stage jobs, forcing inefficient job chaining
materializing intermediate map outputs may add overhead that outweighs locality savings
data skew on hot keys can create stragglers that simple backup tasks cannot fix
awkward interaction with global state or multi-step joins may break the abstraction
failure recovery may still be too slow for short jobs with frequent node outages
locality may be poor when filesystem replication placement and task scheduling are not coordinated
bet.generalizationBoundary: The abstraction is intended for batch jobs expressible as per-record transformations followed by grouping/aggregation; it may not generalize well to streaming data, iterative graph algorithms, interactive queries, or pipelines requiring fine-grained multi-stage coordination without composing multiple map/reduce jobs.
unresolvedUnknowns: Can map/reduce match or approach manual pipeline performance on locality-sensitive production jobs?
How should intermediate data be partitioned and scheduled to preserve locality under node failure?
Does the simple map/reduce model cover a large enough fraction of team workloads to justify centralizing it?
How should key skew and load imbalance be handled robustly without programmer intervention?
What is the right division of responsibility between the distributed filesystem and the map/reduce runtime?
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed actions use only commodity Linux clusters, the existing fault-tolerant distributed filesystem, custom batch schedulers and workers, partition/group/aggregate code, and measurement of production-like jobs; no unavailable technologies or future named outcomes are assumed.

records.cutoff: late 2003, after large commodity clusters and a fault-tolerant distributed filesystem are described, before the MapReduce publication

bet.dominantBottleneck: Programmers repeatedly rebuild partitioning, scheduling, failure handling, and straggler management for each batch job, preventing reuse and underutilizing the distributed filesystem's locality and fault-tolerance features.

routes.route: MapReduce-style two-phase abstraction
routes.reason: Closely matches the observed scan, transform, and group/aggregate workload pattern and naturally leverages the fault-tolerant distributed filesystem for locality and restartable tasks.

routes.route: SQL/relational layer over the cluster
routes.reason: High-level but forces declarative queries and type schemas that do not cover custom transformation code; postpone until the simpler abstraction is characterized.

routes.route: Shared scheduler but app-managed dataflow
routes.reason: Would improve resource sharing but leave per-job partitioning, movement, retries, and straggler logic in the applications, failing to remove the main duplication.

routes.route: Distributed shared-memory style object store
routes.reason: Does not match coarse-grained batch scans/aggregations on large files and would impose too much fine-grained coordination overhead.

bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Implement a minimal MapReduce-style runtime using the existing fault-tolerant distributed filesystem and compare it against three hand-written production-like batch jobs, measuring end-to-end throughput, data locality hit rate, and recovery latency under randomized worker failure injection.

deterministic intermediate-materialization and atomic task output
master-worker scheduling with on-failure reexecution
straggler detection and duplicate-task dispatch

instrumentation for throughput, locality, and failure-recovery metrics

The overhead of coordination and intermediate write may not be repaid for small or short-running jobs
A single phase of grouping may create skew when one key dominates the aggregation

bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed actions use only commodity Linux clusters, the existing fault-tolerant distributed filesystem, custom scheduler/worker processes, and measurement instrumentation; no unavailable tools or future outcomes are assumed.

records.cutoff: late 2003, after large commodity clusters and a fault-tolerant distributed filesystem are described, before the MapReduce publication

bet.dominantBottleneck: Application teams are spending most of their effort re-implementing distributed batch infrastructure: partitioning, scheduling, failure recovery, and locality-aware movement are duplicated in every job, obscuring the common map/aggregate structure inside bespoke systems code.

routes.route: Build a MapReduce-style batch abstraction with automatic partitioning, scheduling, retries, and locality-aware execution on top of the existing distributed filesystem.
routes.reason: The evidence strongly suggests most jobs are local transformations followed by grouping or aggregation, and a centralized runtime can hide failure handling while exploiting block locality and custom user functions.

routes.route: Build a SQL-like declarative layer over the same cluster filesystem, reusing relational optimization and joins.
routes.reason: Relational systems offer advanced optimization but impose schema/query constraints and do not directly match custom record-at-a-time transformations in many web-scale batch jobs; revisit after map-style pilots reveal expression gaps.

routes.route: Build a general DAG dataflow engine with arbitrary user-defined operators and explicit edges.
routes.reason: More expressive, but the scheduling, checkpointing, and execution semantics are far larger design surface; first test whether the restricted MapReduce-style pattern covers the actual workload before expanding generality.

routes.route: Provide a shared scheduler and retry library without imposing a processing abstraction.
routes.reason: It reduces duplicate retry logic but leaves partitioning and data-flow assembly to each team, so the core bottleneck of per-application distributed data plumbing remains.

bet.topRoute: Build a MapReduce-style batch abstraction with automatic partitioning, scheduling, retries, and locality-aware execution on top of the existing distributed filesystem.
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Implement a minimal MapReduce-style runtime and run three production-representative jobs (an inverted indexer, a large-scale grep/count, and a distributed sort) on a 500-node commodity cluster; compare end-to-end latency, data-locality hit rate, user-code size, and recovery time against the same jobs manually implemented with the existing scheduler and filesystem, while injecting 5% random worker failures to observe straggler and retry behavior.
requiredComplements: Fault-tolerant distributed filesystem with block replication and locality-aware reads
Cluster batch scheduler that can place tasks on machines holding relevant input data
Task status and retry service that re-executes failed or in-progress tasks
A shuffle/partitioning mechanism to group intermediate key-value pairs
User-defined function API for custom map and reduce logic
Instrumentation for measuring locality, throughput, straggler distribution, and recovery cost
mainFailureRisks: MapReduce-style abstraction may be too narrow: multi-stage joins, iterative algorithms, and some transformations do not fit naturally, pushing users into awkward compositions.
Runtime overhead from sorting, serialization, and intermediate data materialization may dominate for small or simple jobs, making the abstraction not repay its cost.
Input/output side effects in user functions can cause duplicate writes or inconsistent results when tasks are re-executed after failures.
Data skew may create stragglers that undermine locality benefits; simple backup tasks may not always recover performance.
Measuring programmer effort is subjective and hard to quantify, so the claimed reduction in duplicated logic may not be empirically clean.
bet.generalizationBoundary: The proposed abstraction is intended for large-scale, one-shot batch workloads over record-oriented files where processing can be expressed as an independent map phase followed by key-based grouping and aggregation; it is not claimed to cover low-latency interactive queries, strict multi-way joins with cost-based optimization, ACID transactions, iterative graph algorithms, or streaming-forever computations unless later extended with composable operators and incremental update mechanisms.
unresolvedUnknowns: What fraction of the existing production job mix actually fits the map/group/aggregate shape?
Can one runtime reach near-manual performance for locality and failure recovery without extensive per-job tuning?
How should multi-stage pipelines be expressed and optimized while keeping fault-tolerance simple?
How does the abstraction handle non-key-value workloads such as branching, side outputs, or random-access updates?
What straggler mitigation strategies are robust under different skew distributions?
Does sequential file I/O and bulk recomputation remain acceptable for jobs that need small incremental updates?
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed next actions use only commodity Linux clusters, the existing fault-tolerant distributed filesystem, locally implemented batch schedulers and worker processes, and standard job throughput/locality/failure measurements; no unavailable future tools or named post-cutoff outcomes are assumed.

records.cutoff: 2010, after programmable GPUs and ImageNet are available, before the 2012 AlexNet result

bet.dominantBottleneck: Optimizing and regularizing deep CNNs at ImageNet scale with bounded compute; conventional features still dominate, so it is unclear whether deep learning can produce held-out gains.

routes.route: End-to-end deep CNN on ImageNet with heavy regularization
routes.reason: Directly confronts the core uncertainty: can a deep supervised network beat established hand-crafted features on a large-scale held-out benchmark within practical compute limits.

routes.route: Unsupervised pretraining and fine-tuning
routes.reason: Pretraining is a plausible complement, but its value is unproven and it consumes compute; first measure the supervised CNN baseline without it to avoid conflating factors.

routes.route: Strong hand-crafted feature baseline as primary system
routes.reason: This is the incumbent approach with limited improvement headway; it should serve as an evaluation control, not the main research bet.

routes.route: Hybrid CNN features plus linear SVM
routes.reason: Useful later to separate feature quality from end-to-end training benefits, but not the primary route because it may underuse backpropagation for joint optimization.

routes.route: Bounded multi-GPU distributed CNN training
routes.reason: Necessary to scale experiments under practical time constraints; it enables the primary route rather than being an independent alternative.

records.cutoff: 2010, after programmable GPUs and ImageNet are available, before the 2012 AlexNet result

bet.dominantBottleneck: Practical large-scale supervised training of deep convolutional networks without overfitting, constrained by compute, optimization difficulty, and limited generalization to held-out benchmark data.

routes.route: Supervised deep CNN with aggressive data augmentation and dropout

routes.route: Conventional feature encoding (Fisher vectors / sparse coding) with linear SVM
routes.reason: Must be kept as a strong baseline for comparison, since conventional vision systems dominate benchmarks and may outperform deep models at this scale.

routes.route: Hybrid CNN features plus linear classifier
routes.reason: Potentially useful if deep features underperform in the final classifier, but premature until the supervised CNN itself is evaluated.

routes.route: Multi-GPU parallel synchronous SGD with learning-rate annealing
routes.reason: Needed to make deep CNN training practical within experiment time; careful synchronous SGD preserves reproducibility and allows scaling to the full dataset.

bet.topRoute: Supervised deep CNN with aggressive data augmentation and dropout
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Compare held-out top-5 accuracy on a 100-class / 100k-image subset between the supervised deep CNN and the conventional feature baseline, with matched training time budgets and the same evaluation protocol; if CNN is competitive or better, scale to full benchmark.
requiredComplements: GPU-optimized convolution kernels
Data augmentation pipeline (crops, flips, color jitter)
Dropout and weight decay
Learning-rate schedule with validation-based early stopping
Held-out evaluation harness for the benchmark
mainFailureRisks: Deep CNN fails to converge due to poor initialization or unstable learning dynamics
Overfitting on the training set despite regularization, hurting held-out accuracy
Training time on the deep CNN exceeds practical experiment budgets
The selected subset benchmark is not predictive of performance on the full benchmark
Unsupervised pretraining, if deferred, turns out to be necessary and requires costly rework
bet.generalizationBoundary: A strong result on this benchmark demonstrates high-capacity image classification on natural images with one thousand classes; it does not imply broad visual or semantic generalization across domains, tasks, or unseen label distributions.
unresolvedUnknowns: Optimal network depth, filter sizes, and layer width
Whether unsupervised pretraining provides significant benefit for supervised CNNs at scale
How to set augmentation and dropout intensities to maximize validation accuracy
How closely subset scaling curves extrapolate to million-scale training data
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed actions stay within availableCapabilities: training CNNs with backprop, programming contemporary CUDA GPUs, using ImageNet-scale data with held-out evaluation, applying regularization/data augmentation, and comparing against conventional vision baselines.

routes.route: Develop CTLA-4 blockade as lead candidate

routes.route: Develop PD-1-pathway blockade as parallel candidate
routes.reason: Strong biological rationale in exhaustion and peripheral tolerance; needs head-to-head comparison with CTLA-4 for safety and durability.

routes.route: Develop combination CTLA-4 plus PD-1 blockade
routes.reason: Potential for greater efficacy but higher autoimmune risk and added complexity; should follow lead-candidate identification.

bet.topRoute: Develop CTLA-4 blockade as lead candidate

Autoimmune toxicity monitoring in animal models and patients
Tumor-type-specific response analysis
Biomarker/immunology assays to identify responsive populations
mainFailureRisks: Severe immune-related adverse events undermining risk-benefit
Tumor types responding differently, limiting broad applicability
Early tumor shrinkage not translating into durable survival benefit
Combination regimens amplifying toxicity without proportional efficacy gain
bet.generalizationBoundary: Findings from selected animal tumor models may not generalize across all tumor types or to combination dosing schedules in humans.

records.cutoff: 2005, after inhibitory immune receptors and early CTLA-4 clinical translation are known, before PD-1 phase-I development and later multi-tumor response evidence

bet.dominantBottleneck: The lack of validated clinical/biological decision rules to distinguish durable survival benefit from early tumor shrinkage and to predict serious immune toxicity in small early-phase trials.

routes.route: Parallel single-agent development of anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1/PD-L1 in advanced cancers
routes.reason: Both checkpoints have independent biological rationale; parallel evaluation preserves candidate diversity and allows direct comparison of antitumor durability and immune toxicity without confounding.

routes.route: Combination blockade of CTLA-4 and PD-1/PD-L1 as initial phase I/II strategy
routes.reason: Combining two unproven immunotherapies before understanding single-agent activity and toxicity risks overlapping autoimmunity and prevents attribution of benefit or harm to either pathway.

routes.route: Biomarker-restricted enrollment based on tumor PD-L1 expression or T-cell infiltration
routes.reason: The predictive value of such biomarkers is not yet validated; restricting enrollment early may miss responsive biomarker-negative patients and delay toxicity/safety profiling.

routes.route: Preclinical autoimmunity and therapeutic-index screening to select a single lead candidate
routes.reason: Animal autoimmunity models are unlikely to predict human immune-related adverse events or antitumor efficacy, so further animal prioritization would not resolve the principal clinical bottleneck.

routes.route: Combining checkpoint blockade with vaccine/cytokine immune stimulation
routes.reason: Prior vaccine/immune-stimulation approaches have frequently disappointed, and adding such agents to checkpoint blockade would complicate attribution and toxicity without strong evidence in the packet.

bet.topRoute: Parallel single-agent development of anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1/PD-L1 in advanced cancers
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Randomized phase II trial in advanced melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer assigning patients to anti-CTLA-4 or anti-PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy, with mandatory baseline tumor biopsies, standardized immune toxicity management, co-primary endpoints of 6-month durable response and grade 3-4 immune-toxicity rate, and pre-planned go/no-go rules for advancing the superior arm or later testing combination.
requiredComplements: Standardized immune-related response criteria that capture delayed/atypical responses after initial progression
Pre-specified immune adverse event management algorithms and independent safety monitoring
Mandatory baseline and on-treatment tumor and blood biospecimens for biomarker/immunology correlatives
Prospective definition of durable survival (e.g., landmark survival at 12-24 months) before unblinding
Pre-planned decision rules to move from single-agent signals to a randomized combination trial only after observed single-agent toxicity/activity
mainFailureRisks: Serious immune adverse events leading to treatment-related deaths or trial termination
Low or absent objective responses in unselected patients causing premature abandonment of an active agent
Heterogeneous tumor biology across histologies obscures a true signal present in one subset
Early tumor shrinkage misleads while durable survival is not improved, or vice versa
Biomarker-correlative assays are not analytically validated and yield non-reproducible results
Combination therapy, if eventually tested, produces overlapping/unacceptable autoimmunity without meaningful added efficacy
bet.generalizationBoundary: Results should be generalized only to the specific tumor types, patient populations, and anti-CTLA-4/anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibody clones tested; they cannot be extrapolated to all cancers, other checkpoint molecules, combination sequences, or unmeasured long-term autoimmune sequelae.
unresolvedUnknowns: Whether PD-1/PD-L1 blockade is clinically active in humans with acceptable safety
Optimal dose, schedule, and serum exposure for each antibody candidate
Which patients are most likely to derive durable benefit versus severe toxicity
Relationship between baseline tumor PD-L1 expression or T-cell infiltration and clinical outcomes
Whether durable responses can be achieved without continuous dosing and with manageable autoimmune off-tumor effects
Mechanisms of primary and acquired resistance to single-agent checkpoint blockade
Whether combination blockade has additive efficacy without prohibitive autoimmunity
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed actions use only listed capabilities: monoclonal antibody production, animal tumor/autoimmunity models, early-phase oncology trials, independent response/survival/toxicity measurement, separate CTLA-4 and PD-1-pathway candidates, and biomarker/immunology assays; no unlisted future tools or post-cutoff outcomes are assumed.

records.cutoff: 2005, after inhibitory immune receptors and early CTLA-4 clinical translation are known, before PD-1 phase-I development and later multi-tumor response evidence

bet.dominantBottleneck: The dominant bottleneck is the uncertain safety-efficacy trade-off between available checkpoint targets; strong preclinical efficacy for one inhibitory receptor does not ensure a manageable autoimmune profile, and early response may not predict durable benefit.

routes.route: Develop PD-1-pathway blockade as monotherapy
routes.reason: The PD-1 pathway is implicated in peripheral immune tolerance and T-cell exhaustion, and its distinct biology may provide a better therapeutic index than CTLA-4 blockade; monotherapy data will establish a safety and activity baseline.

routes.route: Develop CTLA-4 blockade as monotherapy
routes.reason: CTLA-4 has strong animal anti-tumor data but carries a high risk of severe autoimmunity; hold as a single agent until head-to-head animal therapeutic-index data justify its advancement.

routes.route: Combine CTLA-4 and PD-1 blockade upfront
routes.reason: Combination could improve efficacy but may amplify immune toxicity and cannot be rationally designed without independent monotherapy safety and activity data from the same model system.

routes.route: Develop biomarker-guided patient selection for PD-1-pathway blockade
routes.reason: Biomarkers such as baseline immune infiltration or exhaustion markers measurable by available assays may separate responders from non-responders and should be incorporated from the earliest trials.

bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Run parallel animal tumor/autoimmunity studies comparing PD-1-pathway blockade versus CTLA-4 blockade, measuring anti-tumor response and autoimmune severity separately, to verify that PD-1-pathway blockade offers a superior therapeutic index before expanding human trials.
requiredComplements: Independent data safety monitoring board for early-phase oncology trials
Preclinical combination toxicity study before any CTLA-4/PD-1 combination
Companion biomarker assay for tumor PD-L1 and immune infiltration using available immunology tools
Prespecified durability endpoints such as progression-free survival and overall survival, separate from objective response rate
mainFailureRisks: Severe autoimmune adverse events requiring treatment discontinuation
No durable benefit despite early objective responses
Low response rates in tumor types lacking pre-existing immune infiltration
Resistance via alternative immune checkpoints or immunosuppressive cells
bet.generalizationBoundary: Any efficacy and safety conclusions apply only to the tumor types and biomarker-defined patient subgroups studied; they should not be generalized to all cancers without independent validation.
unresolvedUnknowns: Optimal dose and schedule for PD-1-pathway blockade
Predictive biomarkers beyond PD-L1 and immune infiltration
Long-term durability and survival impact
Whether combination with CTLA-4 can be made safe and more effective
Mechanisms of primary and acquired resistance
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: All proposed actions use only listed capabilities: monoclonal antibody production, animal tumor/autoimmunity models, early-phase oncology trials, independent measurement of tumor response/survival/durability/toxicity, independent CTLA-4/PD-1 candidates, and available biomarker/immunology assays.
